clinicalPearls: Sarcomas are rare (<1% of all malignancies) mesenchymal neoplasms arising in bone and soft tissues, usually of mesodermal origin and biologically distinct from the more common epithelial cancers (p.727).
The most common presentation of a soft tissue sarcoma is an asymptomatic mass; mechanical symptoms from pressure, traction, or entrapment of nerves or muscles may also occur (p.728).

Approximately 60% of soft tissue sarcomas arise in the extremities (lower limbs involved three times as often as upper), 30% in the trunk (retroperitoneum = 40% of trunk lesions), and 10% in the head and neck (p.727).
The pulmonary parenchyma is the most common site of metastasis for soft tissue sarcomas; lung radiograph plus chest CT is important for detecting lung metastases (p.728).
Histologic grade and primary tumor size are the most important prognostic factors; prognosis is related to AJCC stage and cure is common in the absence of metastatic disease (p.728).
About one-third of soft tissue sarcomas carry a characteristic translocation with diagnostic/prognostic relevance (e.g., t(X;18)(p11;q11) involving SYT in ~90% of synovial sarcomas) (p.728).

Most malignant GISTs carry activating c-kit mutations causing ligand-independent KIT receptor tyrosine kinase activation; ~5-10% have PDGFRA mutations, and KIT/PDGFRA wild-type GISTs may show SDH B/C/D mutations (p.728).

Osteosarcoma accounts for almost 45% of bone sarcomas, is a spindle-cell neoplasm producing osteoid/bone, with predilection for metaphyses of long bones (distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal humerus); ~60% occur in the second decade (p.729-730).

Classic osteosarcoma radiographic findings: a destructive moth-eaten lesion, spiculated periosteal reaction (sunburst appearance), and a cuff of periosteal new bone at the soft-tissue mass margin (Codman's triangle) (p.730).
The most important predictive factor for long-term survival in osteosarcoma is response to chemotherapy; long-term survival in extremity osteosarcoma ranges from 60-80% (p.730).

Ewing's sarcoma (~10-15% of bone sarcomas) peaks in the second decade, shows an 'onion peel' periosteal reaction with a soft-tissue mass, expresses p30/32 (MIC-2 product), and carries the t(11;22) translocation fusing fli-1 (chr 11) and ews (chr 22) (p.730).

Chondrosarcoma (~20-25% of bone sarcomas) is a tumor of adulthood/old age (peak 4th-6th decades) with predilection for flat bones (shoulder, pelvic girdles); it has an indolent natural history and is mostly chemoresistant, with surgical resection the mainstay (p.730).
Prostate, breast, and lung primaries account for 80% of all bone metastases; metastatic bone tumors are more common than primary bone tumors (p.730).

Bone is a common metastatic site for prostate, breast, lung, kidney, bladder, and thyroid carcinomas and for lymphomas and sarcomas; in descending frequency the sites are vertebrae, proximal femur, pelvis, ribs, sternum, proximal humerus, and skull (p.730).
When a patient with back pain develops neurologic signs or symptoms, emergency evaluation for spinal cord compression is indicated (p.730).
harrison.pathophysiology: Sarcomas are mesenchymal neoplasms (mostly mesodermal, occasionally neuroectodermal) classified into ~20 groups by their pattern of differentiation toward normal tissue (e.g., rhabdomyosarcoma shows skeletal-muscle cross-striations, leiomyosarcoma shows smooth-muscle spindle fascicles, liposarcoma contains adipocytes). Malignant transformation of benign soft tissue tumors is extremely rare, except that malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (neurofibrosarcoma, malignant schwannoma) can arise from neurofibromas in neurofibromatosis. Etiologic contributors include radiation (tumor arises in the irradiated field, risk rising with time), scar tissue (prior surgery, burn, fracture, foreign body), chemical carcinogens (polycyclic hydrocarbons, asbestos, dioxin), HHV-8 (Kaposi's sarcoma - the only sarcoma virus-associated), and immunodeficiency/immunosuppression. Genetic syndromes include Li-Fraumeni (germline p53), neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1 on chr 17, encoding neurofibromin which inhibits ras), and germline RB1 mutation (chr 13q14, predisposing to osteosarcoma and radiation-unrelated soft tissue sarcomas). About one-third of soft tissue sarcomas carry characteristic translocations; most malignant GISTs have activating c-kit (KIT receptor tyrosine kinase) mutations, fewer have PDGFRA mutations. Bone metastases occur via hematogenous spread (or local invasion); tumors produce osteolytic lesions (via PTH-related peptide, vitamin D-like steroids, prostaglandins, IL-1, TNF inducing osteoclasts) and/or osteoblastic lesions (cytokines activating osteoblasts), with most lesions showing a mix.
additionalDifferentials: Benign soft tissue tumor / well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical lipomatous tumor) - lacks metastatic potential
Benign bone lesions with malignant potential: enchondroma and osteochondroma (to chondrosarcoma); fibrous dysplasia, bone infarcts, Paget's disease (to UPS or osteosarcoma)
Lymphoma, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, and small-cell carcinoma (can be confused with the small round blue cells of Ewing's sarcoma)
Osteoporosis vs metastatic spine disease in older patients (cortical bone preserved in osteoporosis; cortical destruction with metastases)
Plasma cell tumors (the most common malignant tumor of bone)
nonInfectiousMimics: Osteoporotic vertebral disease mimicking spinal bone metastasis in older patients
Benign enchondroma / osteochondroma mimicking low-grade chondrosarcoma (difficult to distinguish by x-ray or histology; new pain, inflammation, or progressive size increase suggests malignancy)
Well-encapsulated benign-appearing lesion produced by the compressed pseudocapsule of a soft tissue sarcoma
additionalInvestigations: Core-needle (cutting needle) or small-incision biopsy of all new, persistent, or growing masses, placed so it can be encompassed in the definitive resection
Plain radiographs and MRI for primary tumors of extremities or head/neck (MRI best for intramedullary and soft-tissue extension)
CT for tumors of the chest, abdomen, or retroperitoneum (CT best for bone destruction and calcification pattern in osteosarcoma)
Chest radiograph and chest CT to detect lung metastases
Bone scan or FDG-PET to detect skeletal metastases (almost all osteosarcomas are hypervascular and PET-avid)
Radionuclide bone scanning (sensitive to new bone formation) for osteoblastic lesions; plain radiography for osteolytic lesions (may not be apparent until >1 cm)
Serum alkaline phosphatase (elevated with prominent osteoblastic activity) and monitoring for hypercalcemia (osteolytic) or hypocalcemia (extensive osteoblastic)
redFlags: An enlarging, deep, or large soft tissue mass requires biopsy - all new, persistent, or growing masses should be biopsied rather than ignored
Back pain with new neurologic signs or symptoms mandates emergency evaluation for spinal cord compression
New onset of pain, signs of inflammation, and progressive size increase in a cartilaginous lesion suggest malignant (chondrosarcoma) transformation
Bone pain that develops gradually over weeks, is localized, and is more severe at night suggests bone metastasis
Pathologic fracture, nerve root or cord compression, or myelophthisis from a destructive bony lesion
Hypercalcemia symptoms in the setting of bony destruction
harrison.prognosis: For soft tissue sarcoma, histologic grade and size are the most important prognostic factors and prognosis tracks AJCC stage; cure is common without metastatic disease, and a small number with metastases can still be cured. Metastatic soft tissue sarcomas are largely incurable, but up to 20% achieving complete response become long-term survivors. Historically most stage IV patients died within 12 months, but with multiple treatment lines, median survival in second-line and beyond is now 13-18 months and some live with stable/slowly progressive disease for years. Extremity osteosarcoma long-term survival is 60-80%, with response to chemotherapy the key predictor. Ewing's sarcoma overall cure rates approach 60-70% for localized tumors. For bone metastases, overall survival is related to the prognosis of the underlying tumor; some (lymphoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma) are curable while most are treated palliatively.
pitfalls: Soft tissue sarcomas grow along fascial planes and compress surrounding tissue into a pseudocapsule, giving a deceptive well-encapsulated appearance; 'shelling out' (marginal excision / enucleation) results in a 50-90% probability of local recurrence - wide excision with a negative margin incorporating the biopsy site is standard.

A biopsy of an enlarging/deep/large mass must be planned so the tract can be encompassed in the definitive resection and does not compromise a limb-sparing operation; an inappropriately placed incision compromises future limb salvage.
Low-grade chondrosarcoma is difficult to distinguish from benign lesions on x-ray or histology, so diagnosis is influenced by clinical history and examination.
Osteosarcoma is radioresistant - radiation therapy has no role in routine management.

Forgetting non-pulmonary metastatic patterns: GISTs metastasize to liver, myxoid liposarcomas seek fatty tissue (retroperitoneum, mediastinum, subcutaneous), clear cell sarcomas may go to bone, and alveolar soft part sarcoma to CNS.
In older patients (especially women), metastatic spine disease must be distinguished from osteoporosis - cortical bone is preserved in osteoporosis but destroyed by metastatic cancer.
harrison.severityClassification: Soft tissue sarcomas use the AJCC (8th edition) TNM/grade system: T1 (<=5 cm), T2 (>5-10 cm), T3 (>10-15 cm), T4 (>15 cm); N0/N1; M0/M1; with grade G1-G3 driving stage grouping (e.g., Stage IA = T1 N0 M0 G1; Stage IV = any T N1 M0, or any T any N M1). Bone sarcomas use the Musculoskeletal Tumor Society system (stage I low grade, II high grade, III nodal/distant metastases; A = intracompartmental, B = extracompartmental) and a TNM system: T1 (<=8 cm), T2 (>8 cm), T3 (discontinuous tumors in the primary bone); M1a (lung) vs M1b (other sites); grade G1-G4 (Ewing's always G4).
management: Wide surgical excision with clear margins as the mainstay of localised disease, planned around a correctly placed biopsy tract.
Radiotherapy in the neoadjuvant or adjuvant setting to improve local control, particularly for high-grade or large limb tumours.
Anthracycline-based chemotherapy with doxorubicin, often combined with ifosfamide, for high-grade, chemosensitive or metastatic disease.
Pulmonary metastasectomy for resectable lung metastases, the commonest site of spread, in selected patients.
Surveillance with clinical review, cross-sectional imaging of the primary site and chest imaging for lung metastases, stratified by grade and stage.
Manage through a specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team from diagnosis, given the rarity and histological complexity.
Early palliative and systemic-therapy input for unresectable metastatic disease, which is largely incurable.
